title: Each held a part
hook: the blind men and the elephant, read whole

segments.voice: Yesterday: Meghiya in the mango grove. Your line: a good friend comes first. Today, a story you've met before, read from its home in the Udana.

Water pot. Winnowing basket. Plowshare. Broom. Each blind man touches one part of the elephant and names it. You heard this story on day three hundred fifty-eight. It turns up on posters and in classrooms, and other traditions tell it too. But short retellings often keep only the middle, and drop how it starts and how it ends. Today we read it whole, from the sixth chapter of the Udana, and listen for three things the short version leaves out: who it was told to, the line about the king, and the verse.
screen: `WATER POT, BASKET, PLOWSHARE, BROOM.` → `SHORT VERSIONS KEEP THE MIDDLE.` → `TODAY, THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The monks come back from town troubled. Teachers of many groups are arguing: is the world eternal or not, finite or not, is the soul the same as the body, does one who is awakened exist after death? And they're wounding each other, the text says, with mouths like daggers. So the story is told to monks, about a city full of argument. Second, the king. After the blind men fight with their fists, the text says simply that the king was delighted. Why? It doesn't explain. Some readers hear a man enjoying a spectacle he arranged; others hear the delight of someone who sees the whole while the others see parts. The text leaves it open. And notice something easy to miss: none of the men lied. The one at the ear really did feel a winnowing basket. Each report was true about its part. What went wrong was the word only. Third, the verse the Buddha speaks after the story. Some teachers and seekers, it says, are attached to these views. They quarrel and dispute, people who see just one side. The problem isn't seeing a part; everyone sees a part. The problem is clinging, and then fighting. Last time the lesson was: hear out a view you dislike. Today goes further: listen to the whole, before you judge.
screen: `MOUTHS LIKE DAGGERS.` · `THE KING WAS DELIGHTED.` · `NO ONE LIED; THE WORD WAS ONLY.` · `PEOPLE WHO SEE ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `EACH HELD A PART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent moment when you made up your mind about someone before they'd finished talking, and replay it slowly. What part were they holding, and what part were you, and is there a word only hiding in your own view? Don't argue it out; let both parts sit side by side, and breathe.
Ditthi, a view or opinion. In Udana 6.4, every blind man's report was true about his part; the quarrel came from clinging to one side. Today's word.
Your line: listen to the whole. Every report was true; the trouble was the word only. Day six hundred nineteen, done.

screen: `DAY 619 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOTHS AND THE LAMP.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the elephant story when teaching about clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in Jain, Hindu and Sufi traditions, each with its own lesson.

fork.setup: you're one of the men who touched the elephant's ear. you're sure it's like a winnowing basket. another man insists it's like a post. what does the verse warn against?
options: clinging to your side and fighting over it.
fork.reveal: everyone touches a part. the verse names those who cling to one side and quarrel as the ones who go wrong.

original.note: Pali ditthi: a view, an opinion. in Udana 6.4 the teachers cling to their ditthi.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story says everyone is a little bit right.
what it means: each report was true about its part; the fault was clinging to one side and fighting over it.
what a scholar hears: Udana 6.4 lists the ten undeclared questions as the teachers' disputes, and is followed by two more suttas (6.5, 6.6) with the same frame.

chat.says: Isn't the elephant story just saying every opinion is equally right?
options: Each man was right about his part; the trouble was saying 'only mine is right,' then fighting.
Yes: every view is equally true, so nobody should ever weigh one against another.
It says the blind men lied about the elephant so they could win the argument.
chat.meaning: In Udana 6.4 none of the men lied; each report fit its part. The verse faults clinging to one side, then quarreling.

Udana.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's inspired sayings
